item.title: Ep 1 · Ch 1 — The Early Church's Search for a Secure Base
item.description:
Chapter 1: Early Christianity: The Patristic Period, c.100–c.700
Reads the Patristic period as a family system stabilizing itself under threat: the Arian controversy as a couple fighting over content instead of the underlying attachment longing, and the creed as an enactment of shared reality. Listeners get the Irenaeus Anchor, Athanasius Reframe, and Cyprian Boundary as in-session lines.

item.title: Ep 2 · Ch 1 — Defining the Canon, Defending Boundaries, Co-Creating a Creed
item.description:
Chapter 1: Early Christianity: The Patristic Period, c.100–c.700
A three-step clinical flow for fractured systems: establish the couple's agreed-upon facts and core memories, protect the therapeutic space from intellectualized distortion, then guide clients to state their commitment out loud. Includes the Pelagian red flag—clients trying to fix the cycle on willpower alone.

item.title: Ep 3 · Ch 1 — Arian, Gnostic, and Donatist Traps in Couples Work
item.description:
Chapter 1: Early Christianity: The Patristic Period, c.100–c.700
Three patristic heresies as diagnostic shorthand for clinical stuck points: minimizing the bond, intellectualizing away the emotion, and demanding perfection before repair. Each comes with the attachment fear it defends and a specific intervention to restore embodied connection.

item.title: Ep 4 · Ch 2 — The Great Schism as Pursuer-Withdrawer Rupture
item.description:
Chapter 2: The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, c.700–c.1500
Uses the 1054 East-West split to show how one partner builds intellectual "cathedrals" of logic and proof while the other retreats into wordless mystery — a macro-scale pursue-withdraw cycle. Listeners learn to bypass the content argument (the couple's own filioque debate) and access the attachment panic driving both defenses.

item.title: Ep 5 · Ch 2 — Ad Fontes: Returning to the Primary Emotion
item.description:
Chapter 2: The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, c.700–c.1500
Borrows the Renaissance humanist move of going back to the original source text and applies it to couples who are working from corrupted translations of each other's behavior. Gives a three-step workflow for spotting the bad translation, finding the raw attachment need underneath, and refusing to hand out behavioral homework in place of emotional contact.

item.title: Ep 6 · Ch 2 — Correcting the Mistranslations That Fuel the Cycle
item.description:
Chapter 2: The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, c.700–c.1500
Focuses on the specific error of reading withdrawal as "he doesn't care" rather than "he's overwhelmed," and how the therapist becomes the room's new translator. Includes practice steps for surfacing a client's internal translation dictionary and converting behavioral demands ("she wants me to grovel") into attachment longings.

item.title: Ep 7 · Ch 2 — Hesychasm: Inner Stillness as the Therapist's Anchor
item.description:
Chapter 2: The Middle Ages and the Renaissance, c.700–c.1500
Turns to the self of the therapist, using the Byzantine practice of inner quietness as a model for staying regulated while a couple escalates. Covers the trap of rushing to fill silence, and Palamas's energy/essence distinction as a way to hold a client's anger without mistaking it for who they are.

item.title: Ep 8 · Ch 3 — Reformation as Attachment Injury with the Divine
item.description:
Chapter 3: The Age of Reformation, c.1500–c.1750
Reads the Reformation as a systemic restructuring of a mediated attachment bond: works-righteousness as anxious attachment, Luther as pursuer, Anabaptism as radical differentiation, and Trent as the system's defensive boundary-setting. Listeners learn to track the process (the search for a secure base) rather than getting caught in the content of doctrine.

item.description:
Chapter 3: The Age of Reformation, c.1500–c.1750

Includes the red flag of "confessionalization" — partners rigidly stating beliefs to intellectualize relational panic.

Listeners learn to recognize the hyper-rational client who builds a logical case in place of feeling, and how the EFT Tango moves them from evidence-gathering to the attachment fear underneath. Includes language for naming intellectualization as protection rather than debating it.

item.description:
Chapter 4: The Modern Period, c.1750 to the Present

item.description:
Chapter 5: Getting Started: Preliminaries
The distinction between believed content and the act of trusting maps directly onto clients who can recite the rules of good communication but stay emotionally disconnected. Learn to spot intellectual understanding functioning as a defense and use the EFT Tango to move a couple from knowing the steps to risking the lean.

item.description:

A client's cultural or religious stance often mirrors their attachment strategy at a macro level, so rigid ideology in the room is a shield rather than an enemy. Learn to validate the fear driving the belief instead of debating it, and to use the client's own spiritual language to frame attachment needs.

item.description:
Chapter 5: Getting Started: Preliminaries
When partners argue like lawyers, citing evidence and delivering perfectly logical summaries, the session goes cold and gridlocked. Learn to name intellectualization as a coping strategy, validate the logic to lower the defense, then pivot to the body and the desperate plea underneath the facts.

item.description:

The therapist who offers a tissue or a cognitive question the moment a client sobs is soothing themselves, not the client. Learn to recognize your own attachment alarm behind your model preferences and build the capacity to stay in the emotional fire without rescuing or teaching.

item.title: Ep 20 · Ch 6 — The Wesleyan Quadrilateral as an Attachment Map
item.description:
Chapter 6: The Sources of Theology
Listeners learn to hear Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience as attachment strategies — external secure bases or defenses against abandonment fear — rather than as content to debate. The episode walks the EFT Tango through a client who deflects with "God is in control," validating the function of the belief while opening the emotion beneath it.

Listeners get the interception move for when a client quotes a source, the red flag of a tearful moment snapping into rigid doctrine, and five practice steps for the coming week.

item.description:
Chapter 6: The Sources of Theology
Covers what to do when partners weaponize theological authority — one correcting the other's feelings with "the Bible says fear not" — and how rigid canons in a marriage function as a bid for safety and certainty. Listeners learn to drop beneath the theological debate and get the pursuing partner to risk the fear under the demand.

Listeners learn to run the EFT Tango internally — noticing the body signal, naming the activated emotion, and re-grounding before responding.

item.description:
Chapter 7: Knowledge of God: Natural and Revealed

Covers tracking the micro-expressions that contradict a client's angry words, and the red flag of trying to convince someone to feel.

item.description:

Frames the therapist's dual awareness through the Two Books metaphor: the Book of Scripture is the EFT and attachment map, while the Book of Nature is the client's breathing, posture, and silence in the room. Shows how to notice when a brilliant conceptualization has cost you the client, and how to pivot back to somatic tracking.

Listeners learn to spot intellectualization in session and pivot from debating causes to naming the longing for secure connection underneath.

item.title: Ep 29 · Ch 8 — Halting the Forensic Search for Relational First Causes
item.description:
Chapter 8: Philosophy and Theology: Dialogue and Debate

Includes red-flag markers ("logically," "objectively true") and rehearsal steps for interrupting cold, courtroom-style sessions.

item.description:
Chapter 9: The Doctrine of God
The Hellenistic impassible God parallels the blank-slate analyst, and both fail clients who need proof their pain can be held. Listeners learn to let themselves be emotionally impacted, to name the weight they feel in the room, and to stay anchored without retreating into clinical detachment.

Chapter 9: The Doctrine of God
Clients meet betrayal and abuse with soul-making stories, blame, or raw protest, and therapists who chase silver linings invalidate the terror underneath. Learn to validate the protest, drop the search for a good reason, and move the client from cognitive meaning-making to attachment grief.

Listeners learn to trade coercion for invitation, to read resistance as systemic information rather than personal failure, and to validate the protective function of a refused enactment.

item.description:
Chapter 10: The Person of Jesus Christ
Uses the New Testament titles—Messiah, Son of God, Son of Man, Lord, Savior—as a lens on self-of-the-therapist work, especially the rescuer role that drives burnout and client passivity. A self-directed EFT tango for relinquishing the "Savior" identity and sitting in shared human limitation while still holding hope.

item.description:
Chapter 11: The Nature and Basis of Salvation
Explores how a client's implicit theory of the cross — transaction, punishment, or rescue — functions as an internalized working model for how ruptured bonds get repaired. Shows how to bypass the theological content and contact the attachment panic beneath "I have to pay for what I've done."

item.description:
Chapter 11: The Nature and Basis of Salvation
Maps the chapter's three atonement frameworks — satisfaction, sacrifice, and Christus Victor — onto stages of trauma recovery: acknowledging harm, risking costly vulnerability, and overcoming internalized shame. Gives concrete moves for shifting a session's felt sense from judgment to safety, plus markers for spiritual bypassing.

item.description:
Chapter 11: The Nature and Basis of Salvation
Troubleshoots the client whose belief that suffering is required for forgiveness sabotages repair and blocks compassionate connection. Teaches why arguing with the rigid theology only tightens the armor, and how validating the protective function of guilt opens the way to mourning sorrow.

item.description:
Chapter 11: The Nature and Basis of Salvation
Addresses the therapist's countertransference when a client speaks of blood, sacrifice, and divine wrath — the urge to debate, rescue, or go silent. Offers grounding, bridging, and supervision practices for staying with the client's process instead of reacting to the religious content.

item.title: Ep 45 · Ch 12 — Relational Asphyxiation and Breathing Life Into the Bond
item.description:
Chapter 12: The Holy Spirit
Treats the attachment bond itself — the living energy between partners — as the client, and shows why a "dead" room signals a suffocating cycle rather than two broken individuals. Listeners learn to name the deadened atmosphere, reach for the primary emotion beneath the rigid pursue/withdraw pattern, and stage an enactment that restores breath to the bond without over-functioning as its sole source of oxygen.

item.title: Ep 46 · Ch 12 — Flattening the Emotional Hierarchy Inside a Couple's Cycle
item.description:
Chapter 12: The Holy Spirit
Maps the power structure in the room — who arbitrates reality, whose emotional experience gets centered — and gives a playbook for blocking that dominance and amplifying the marginalized partner's voice. Listeners get concrete moves: the interruption script, the concession marker (the look-down, the sigh, the fold), and a co-equal enactment that makes both partners' needs weigh the same.

item.title: Ep 47 · Ch 12 — Tolerating the Wild Wind of Primary Emotion
item.description:
Chapter 12: The Holy Spirit
A self-of-therapist episode on the countertransference that fires when a session turns chaotic and your instinct is to shut it down and re-establish control. Listeners learn to recognize the "cessationist" retreat into psychoeducation and worksheets, and instead channel rather than contain a flood of emotion — providing a secure container while trusting the process to do the healing.

item.title: Ep 48 · Ch 13 — Distinct Yet Not Divided: Enmeshment, Isolation, and Perichoresis
item.description:
Chapter 13: The Trinity
Uses the Trinitarian idea of perichoresis (mutual indwelling without loss of distinctness) as a template for secure connection, mapping the heresies of tritheism and modalism onto the isolated "roommate" couple and the enmeshed partner who wears whatever mask is demanded. Listeners get EFT Tango moves that help partners share emotional space without dissolving into each other, plus the subordinationist trap of treating one partner's needs as more foundational.

item.title: Ep 49 · Ch 13 — The Cycle in the Room Is the Revelation
item.description:
Chapter 13: The Trinity
Borrows Rahner's axiom that the economic Trinity is the immanent Trinity to argue that how a couple behaves in session is the relationship, not a report about it. Listeners learn to catch the sigh and the eye roll, link the micro-move to the larger relational fear, and pivot couples out of abstract complaints ("we always communicate poorly") into a live enactment.

item.title: Ep 50 · Ch 13 — Lending Your Nervous System: Therapist as Bond of Love
item.description:
Chapter 13: The Trinity
Draws on Augustine's Spirit-as-bond-of-love to frame the therapist's attuned presence as the temporary glue holding a dysregulated couple together until they can co-regulate on their own. Covers using yourself as a secure base when partners cannot face each other, bridging back to the partner, and the countertransference that makes the "glue" fail.

item.title: Ep 51 · Ch 14 — Imago Dei: Holding Dignity Beneath a Client's Shame
item.description:
Chapter 14: Human Nature, Sin, and Grace
How the doctrine of the image of God and its defacement in the Fall maps onto a client's conviction that they are "damaged goods," and why the therapist's job is to treat the wound to self-concept rather than the behavioral symptoms. Includes EFT Tango moves and enactments for reaching the grief beneath shame.

item.title: Ep 52 · Ch 14 — Loaded Scales: Why Willpower Fails Wounded Clients
item.description:
Chapter 14: Human Nature, Sin, and Grace
The Pelagian-Augustinian debate reframed as a clinical choice between demanding effort and understanding woundedness, with the "loaded scales" metaphor for a will biased toward self-protection by attachment injury. Listeners learn to spot the "they just need to try harder" marker and respond by exploring barriers instead of prescribing effort.

item.description:

Augustine's distinction between prevenient and cooperative grace becomes a sequence for the therapeutic relationship: offer unconditional acceptance before the client earns it, then collaborate on restructuring the bond. Includes red flags for when you have slipped into the posture of judge.

item.description:

Forensic justification — being declared worthy rather than performing for worth — as a lens on the perfectionistic, over-functioning client who fears abandonment if they stop producing. Covers the trap of praising "good therapeutic work" and thereby reinforcing the merit system the client is trying to escape.

item.description:

Uses the biblical models of the church — people of God, community of salvation, body of Christ — plus Brueggemann's phases of Israel's identity to read congregational disillusionment as an attachment injury. Listeners learn to move a client from defending or rejecting the institution toward mourning the idealized church and re-engaging the real, flawed body.

item.description:

Applies Augustine's corpus permixtum answer to the Donatists — the church as a hospital for the sick, not a club for the healthy — to clients who threaten cutoff when a leader or partner fails morally. Listeners get markers for premature separation, therapist-to-self scripts, and practice steps for holding the wheat and the weeds.

item.description:

Listeners learn to access the longing and grief hidden beneath rigid cutoff, and to name the gap between the invisible ideal relationship and the visible one.

item.description:
Chapter 16: The Sacraments
Augustine's definition of a sacrament reframes the therapeutic container: the room, the hour, the therapist's steady presence are outward signs that actually produce inward security. Listeners learn to treat the enactment as an efficacious act rather than a mere symbol, and get language for grounding clients in the physical frame.

Listeners learn the Augustinian pivot — that healing comes from the process and the client's capacity, not the therapist's moral perfection — and how to use their own woundedness as attunement.

The episode walks through pivoting from the theological debate into the underlying fear of losing each other via reflection, softening, and enactment.

Includes the moves for slowing an escalating truth-debate, spotting the urge to mediate theology, and mapping how belief differences drive the pursue/withdraw cycle.

item.description:

item.description:
